title: Apology
tomorrow: she sent the apology. now nothing. should she text again?

cards: An apology text, drafted in the notes app. Typed, deleted, retyped. A but sneaks in, then gets cut.

Apologies tend to get rehearsed before they're said. Luke shows a rehearsal too. A younger son has spent his whole share, ends up feeding pigs, comes to himself, and works out a speech line by line on the road home.
He even has the opening ready. Then he delivers it, and something's missing. The last line of the speech he practiced never gets said.

teach.b: Here's the rehearsal, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee: I am not now worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants." Notice first what isn't in it.
No famine, no bad friends, no bad luck. Just what he did, and to whom, though there really was a famine. Now the delivery.

His father sees him while he's still far off, runs, falls on his neck and kisses him. The son begins: "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, I am not now worthy to be called thy son." And there it stops.
The hired-servant line is gone. Luke doesn't say why. Some readers hear the father cutting in, already calling for the best robe and a ring.

Others hear a son who, inside his father's arms, can't bargain anymore. Either way, the sorry stays and the deal drops out. A real apology names the wrong, and leaves the price of forgiveness to the one forgiving.
Jesus puts this mending even ahead of worship: leave your gift at the altar and "go first to be reconciled to thy brother."
And one way Mass can begin is the Confiteor, whose Latin says mea culpa: through my fault.
Not someone else's, not the stress, not the day.

how: Catholics confess sins to a priest in the sacrament of Penance and receive absolution, and the Confiteor, with its words through my fault, is one form of the penitential act at the start of Mass.

o: owning a wrong plainly, without a defense
explaining why a mistake wasn't your fault
a formal statement read out in public

games.q: the son's two speeches — tap the pairs.
p: make me as one of thy hired servants
stops at not worthy to be called thy son
runs while the son is far off

s: in Luke, the son delivers his rehearsed speech word for word
the line asking to be a hired servant never gets said.
the son's speech in Luke blames the famine
it names only what he did: I have sinned against heaven, and before thee.
Jesus says to leave your gift at the altar and be reconciled first
in Matthew 5: go first to be reconciled to thy brother.

games.q: you borrowed your sister's car and scraped the bumper in a tight parking lot. she's walking over. which apology has no excuses in it?
o: I scraped your bumper. I'm sorry, and I'll pay to fix it.
that lot is ridiculous; anyone would have scraped it.
I'm sorry, but you never told me the sensor was broken.
games.why: the son's speech names what he did and to whom: no famine, no tight lot, no but. making it right is part of the sorry, not a bargain.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you owe someone an apology for, small or old. Shape it into one plain sentence, what you did and to whom, with no because and no bargain attached.
Say it once, quietly, out loud, and listen to whether it sounds true. If it doesn't, cut whatever is defending you.

wordCard.voice: Apology. Naming what you did, and to whom, with no defense attached and no deal on the end.

orig.note: Latin, from the Confiteor: through my fault.

carryVoice: Your line: no excuses. The son kept the sorry and lost the bargain, and the father ran anyway. Until tomorrow.
